title: Fourier imaging of collective spontaneous emission modes in superradiant cold atomic clouds
authors: Adrien Gavalda, Guillaume Tremblier, Martin Poitrinal, Sara Pancaldi, Antoine Browaeys, Igor Ferrier-Barbut
abstract: We measure the spatial pattern associated with the superradiant emission from a cloud of cold 87Rb atoms using Fourier imaging. We observe a highly directional, ring-shaped emission structure, which corresponds to a single collective jump operator associated to the most superradiant mode of the ensemble. Using spatial filtering, we isolate this channel and find the typical superradiant burst with superlinear scaling of the intensity with atom number. We compare our results to two models that describe the competition between the various decay channels, finding good agreement. Our work shows that the collective jump operators introduced by Carmichael et al. [Optics Communications 179, 417 (2000)] can be measured and manipulated.
summary: The study experimentally investigates superradiant emission from cold atomic clouds using Fourier imaging to map out the spatial structure of emitted light. By comparing these measurements with theoretical models, the authors successfully demonstrate that collective spontaneous decay is governed by specific, measurable jump operators. This work advances our understanding of how mode competition dictates the macroscopic dynamics in interacting quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The study aims to experimentally measure and theoretically characterize the collective spontaneous emission modes associated with superradiant decay in cold atomic clouds.
main_result: The authors successfully measured a highly directional, ring-shaped emission pattern corresponding to the most superradiant mode, confirming theoretical predictions regarding the dominance of specific collective jump operators.
method: The research combines Fourier imaging of emitted light with advanced quantum optical modeling using master equations and diagonalization of decay matrices.
model_or_system: The system involves cold $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms in an optical dipole trap, whose superradiant emission is governed by a master equation incorporating collective jump operators derived from the vacuum Green's function. Theoretical analysis models mode competition using bosonic and Lindblad approximations.
key_observables: Spatial pattern of emitted light in the far field (Fourier plane), superlinear scaling of intensity with atom number ($N$), and decay rates ($\Gamma_l$) associated with collective modes.
important_parameters: Cloud sizes ($\sigma_x, \sigma_r$), Rabi frequencies ($\Omega$), and critical atom numbers ($N_c$). The Fresnel number $F$ governs the dependence on cloud geometry.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximating the system using master equations and diagonalizing decay matrices; limitations include discrepancies between bosonic model predictions (e.g., peak intensity scaling) and experimental observations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measured ring-shaped emission pattern, compare calculated vs. initial probability distributions of superradiant modes, and show how the spectral gap ($\Gamma_1/\Gamma_3$) depends on cloud geometry parameters like $\sigma_r$ and $\sigma_x$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from measuring the spatial patterns of emission to analyzing mode competition using bosonic approximations, refining the model with a detailed Lindblad operator, and finally deriving theoretical conditions for superradiance based on eigenvalue analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial experimental validation for advanced theoretical frameworks describing open quantum systems, specifically demonstrating how collective decay dynamics can be mapped onto measurable spectral properties (eigenvalues/decay rates) of the system's environment coupling.

Partially Pumped Collective Emitters.note: The core concept of superradiant decay and mode competition in a controlled atomic ensemble directly relates to the study of collective emitters, especially if one considers the initial excitation or driving mechanism as analogous to partial pumping.
